item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports separating history content, recency, and interaction order in diagnostics. Cascade-guided adversarial training (2024) identifies excessive reliance on temporal information as a robustness weakness. CoDeR (2025) targets demand shifts obscured by noise; CETRec (2025, LLM-based) distinguishes absolute recency from relative ordering. Genetic-algorithm counterfactual explanations (2025) search for minimal history edits that change recommendations. These motivate complementary probes of temporal sensitivity and decision fragility, but do not establish that an isolated purchase represents a genuine preference shift. Sources: [Cascade-guided training](https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/1.9781611978032.85), [CoDeR](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/33379), [CETRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.03047), [minimal counterfactual edits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03606).\n\nSuggested diagnostic synthesis: on training-history prefixes, compare removal of a sustained recent cluster with removal of an isolated interaction, using titles/descriptions to define similarity. Match control edits on interaction count, original position, and training-item popularity. Separate masking from deletion, since deletion also shifts positions; shuffle within a fixed recent window while preserving its item multiset; replace items with popularity-matched alternatives. Keep the next training interaction and candidate set fixed. Measure target-rank change, score-margin change, top-10 overlap, and paired HR@10 differences across prefixes and categories. Include popularity-only and recent-item similarity controls to assess whether apparent sequence sensitivity exceeds simple associations. These are proposed experimental controls, rather than a verified protocol from the cited papers. Interpret results as model sensitivity under specified edits; implausible histories, correlated interactions, and unobserved intent prevent causal identification of user preferences."}
